idea.before:
The diagonalizer $D$ first *marks off* $s(n)$ cells (that is what space-constructibility buys) and then simulates $M_x$ on $x$ inside them. A machine that tries to leave the fence is stopped and answered arbitrarily. A machine that loops would make $D$ loop too, so $D$ also counts steps: a computation confined to $s$ cells can pass through at most $|Q|\cdot s\cdot|\Gamma|^{s}$ distinct configurations, so if it runs longer it repeats one and never halts, and $D$ may stop it and say what it likes. Otherwise $D$ answers the opposite of $M_x$. Any machine using $s'=o(s)$ cells fits inside the fence for long inputs, so $D$ differs from it.

The configuration bound is a product-rule count (comb-1.1): choose the state, each head position and the contents of each bounded tape. These choices describe a configuration even when some combinations are unreachable; counting a superset is enough for the stopping bound.

The pigeonhole principle (comb-1.2) then turns the finite configuration count into a time limit. Once a deterministic run visits more configurations than there are descriptions, two are equal, and their subsequent runs coincide. An accepting or rejecting halt cannot first occur after that repetition.

The diagonalizer $D$ first *marks off* $s(n)$ cells (that is what space-constructibility buys) and then simulates $M_x$ on $x$ inside them. A machine that tries to leave the fence is stopped and answered arbitrarily. A machine that loops would make $D$ loop too, so $D$ also counts steps: for a fixed machine with $k$ work tapes, a length-$n$ read-only input and at most $s$ cells per work tape, there are at most $|Q|(n+2)(s+1)^k|\Gamma|^{ks}$ configurations (state, input-head position, work-head positions and tape symbols), so if it runs longer it repeats one and never halts, and $D$ may stop it and say what it likes. The logarithm of this count is $O(s+\log n)=O(s)$ for the constructible bounds $s\ge\log n$, so the step counter fits in the space budget. Otherwise $D$ answers the opposite of $M_x$. Any machine using $s'=o(s)$ cells fits inside the fence for long inputs, so $D$ differs from it.

The pigeonhole principle (comb-1.2) then turns the finite configuration count into a time limit. Once a deterministic run visits more configurations than there are descriptions, two are equal, and their subsequent runs coincide. An accepting or rejecting halt cannot first occur after that repetition.

idea.before:
**Oracle $A$.** $\mathrm P^A\subseteq\mathrm{NP}^A\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}^A=\mathrm{PSPACE}$ (the whole oracle-using computation is a polynomial-space computation, answering queries by running a PSPACE algorithm), and $\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm P^A$ because $A$ is PSPACE-hard. Concretely, a nondeterministic machine that guesses $y$ and asks $A$ about $\varphi_y$ is simulated by *one* query $\exists y\,\varphi_y$, itself a quantified formula. **Oracle $B$.** $L_B\in\mathrm{NP}^B$: guess a string of length $n$ and query it. Order all polynomial-time oracle machines $M_1,M_2,\dots$ and build $B$ in stages: at stage $i$ choose a fresh length $n_i$ with $2^{n_i}$ larger than $M_i$'s running time, and run $M_i^{B}$ on $1^{n_i}$ with $B$ so far (nothing of length $n_i$). If $M_i$ accepts, leave $B$ empty at that length; then $1^{n_i}\notin L_B$ and $M_i$ is wrong. If it rejects, it queried fewer than $2^{n_i}$ strings, so put an *unqueried* string of length $n_i$ into $B$: the run is unchanged, $M_i$ still rejects, but $1^{n_i}\in L_B$. Every $M_i$ errs somewhere. The key fact in both halves is that oracle machines relativize: the same diagonal argument as 1.2 works, but it can be *aimed* by choosing the oracle.

The required fresh length exists by pma-3.20(d): for each fixed clock $n^d$ and constant $C$, $Cn^d/2^n\to0$. Hence a stage can choose an arbitrarily large length with more candidate strings than queries. This numerical gap leaves an unqueried string; it does not itself prove that later stages preserve earlier oracle answers.
idea.after:
**Oracle $A$.** $\mathrm P^A\subseteq\mathrm{NP}^A\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}^A=\mathrm{PSPACE}$ (the whole oracle-using computation is a polynomial-space computation, answering queries by running a PSPACE algorithm), and $\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm P^A$ because $A$ is PSPACE-hard. Concretely, a nondeterministic machine that guesses $y$ and asks $A$ about $\varphi_y$ is simulated by *one* query $\exists y\,\varphi_y$, itself a quantified formula. **Oracle $B$.** $L_B\in\mathrm{NP}^B$: guess a string of length $n$ and query it. Order all polynomial-time oracle machines $M_1,M_2,\dots$ and build $B$ in stages: at stage $i$ choose a fresh length $n_i$ greater than every earlier chosen or queried length, with $2^{n_i}$ larger than $M_i$'s running time, and run $M_i^{B}$ on $1^{n_i}$ with $B$ so far (nothing of length $n_i$). If $M_i$ accepts, leave $B$ empty at that length; then $1^{n_i}\notin L_B$ and $M_i$ is wrong. If it rejects, it queried fewer than $2^{n_i}$ strings, so put an *unqueried* string of length $n_i$ into $B$: the run is unchanged, $M_i$ still rejects, but $1^{n_i}\in L_B$. Freeze every answer queried at this stage. Later stages choose lengths beyond all these queries and all earlier chosen lengths, so they neither alter this run nor fill an earlier length deliberately left empty. Every $M_i$ errs somewhere. The key fact in both halves is that oracle machines relativize: the same diagonal argument as 1.2 works, but it can be *aimed* by choosing the oracle.

The required fresh length exists by pma-3.20(d): for each fixed clock $n^d$ and constant $C$, $Cn^d/2^n\to0$. Hence a stage can choose an arbitrarily large length with more candidate strings than queries. This numerical gap leaves an unqueried string; it does not itself prove that later stages preserve earlier oracle answers.

statement.before: **Conjecture (Berman–Hartmanis, 1977):** any two NP-complete languages are *polynomial-time isomorphic*: for NP-complete $A,B$ there is a bijection $h:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}^*$ with $x\in A\iff h(x)\in B$ such that both $h$ and $h^{-1}$ are computable in polynomial time. **Theorem (the supporting half):** if $A\le_p B$ and $B\le_p A$ by reductions $f,g$ that are injective, length-increasing and polynomial-time invertible — which holds for every known natural NP-complete set, because *padding* can always be added — then $A$ and $B$ are $p$-isomorphic. All known natural NP-complete problems are $p$-isomorphic to SAT; the conjecture asserts it for all of them. It would imply P $\ne$ NP (if P = NP, a one-element set would be NP-complete and could not be isomorphic to an infinite one) and that no NP-complete set is sparse, since a $p$-isomorphism preserves density up to a polynomial.
statement.after: **Conjecture (Berman–Hartmanis, 1977):** any two NP-complete languages are *polynomial-time isomorphic*: for NP-complete $A,B$ there is a bijection $h:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}^*$ with $x\in A\iff h(x)\in B$ such that both $h$ and $h^{-1}$ are computable in polynomial time. **Theorem (the supporting half):** if $A\le_p B$ and $B\le_p A$ by reductions $f,g$ that are injective, strictly length-increasing and polynomial-time invertible (an inverse procedure finds a preimage or reports that the input is outside the range) — which holds for every known natural NP-complete set, because *padding* can always be added — then $A$ and $B$ are $p$-isomorphic. All known natural NP-complete problems are $p$-isomorphic to SAT; the conjecture asserts it for all of them. It would imply P $\ne$ NP (if P = NP, a one-element set would be NP-complete and could not be isomorphic to an infinite one) and that no NP-complete set is sparse, since a $p$-isomorphism preserves density up to a polynomial.

idea.before:
The theorem is the Schröder–Bernstein argument made efficient. Draw $x\in A$ — $f(x)\in B$ — $g(f(x))\in A$ … as a path; because $f,g$ are injective these paths never branch, and because they increase length they never cycle. Every element lies on a chain whose backward end is either in $A$ (not in the range of $g$) or in $B$ (not in the range of $f$). Define $h(x)=f(x)$ on chains starting in $A$ and $h(x)=g^{-1}(x)$ on chains starting in $B$. Following a chain *backwards* shortens the string at every step and invertibility is polynomial, so $h$ is computable in polynomial time; the same rule runs in reverse for $h^{-1}$. The conjecture itself is open; its truth would mean all NP-complete problems are the same problem in different notation.

The set-theoretic step is the chain pairing in Schröder–Bernstein (logic-1.3), applied to two disjoint copies of the full string universe. It proves bijectivity of the piecewise choice of forward map or backward inverse. Effectiveness is additional: the stated injectivity, strict length increase and polynomial-time inverse checks let one follow a chain backwards for at most its starting length, deciding which copy contains its first point. The classical theorem alone gives no running-time bound.
idea.after:
The theorem is the Schröder–Bernstein argument made efficient. Use two disjoint copies of $\{0,1\}^*$, the source copy labelled $A$ and the target copy labelled $B$, including both members and nonmembers of the languages. Draw $x$ — $f(x)$ — $g(f(x))$ … as a path; because $f,g$ are injective these paths never branch, and because they increase length they never cycle. Every element lies on a chain whose backward end is either in $A$ (not in the range of $g$) or in $B$ (not in the range of $f$). Define $h(x)=f(x)$ on chains starting in $A$ and $h(x)=g^{-1}(x)$ on chains starting in $B$. Following a chain *backwards* uses the inverse procedure and verifies its range claim, shortening the string at every successful step. There are at most $|x|$ backward steps, each on a string of length at most $|x|$, so the root-copy decision and $h$ take polynomial time; the reverse pairing gives $h^{-1}$ with the same bound. Membership is preserved along every edge because $f,g$ are reductions, so the resulting whole-universe bijection also preserves the languages. The conjecture itself is open; its truth would mean all NP-complete problems are the same problem in different notation.

The set-theoretic step is the chain pairing in Schröder–Bernstein (logic-1.3), applied to two disjoint copies of the full string universe. It proves bijectivity of the piecewise choice of forward map or backward inverse. Effectiveness is additional: the stated injectivity, strict length increase and polynomial-time inverse checks let one follow a chain backwards for at most its starting length, deciding which copy contains its first point. The classical theorem alone gives no running-time bound.
